item.title: Airway cross-sectional area measurement using quantitative endoscopy with AI-enabled depth estimation: A proof-of-concept study
item.description: arXiv:2610.20623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Endoscopy is widely used in medicine to visualize anatomical structures for diagnosis and treatment evaluation. However, it does not currently allow rapid, quantitative measurement of airway cross-sectional area (CSA), a key metric for diagnosing and managing respiratory pathologies. There is growing interest in AI-enabled quantitative endoscopy using depth estimation, but a fundamental challenge is the need for ground-truth depth data to train algorithms capable of quantifying depth in physical units (e.g., meters). In this study, 60,000 paired virtual endoscopy images and depth maps were created in Blender from 3D airway models built from computed tomography. A U-Net convolutional neural network was trained to predict the depth maps from the endoscopy images. Point clouds were reconstructed from the AI-generated depth maps using the Equisolid fisheye lens model, and airway perimeters were identified by intersecting a plane with the point cloud to estimate CSA. Nasopharyngeal CSA, a key metric in obstructive sleep apnea, was quantified using this AI-enabled approach with a median error of 5.3 \% relative to the 3D model ground-truth. This pilot study using synthetic data provides strong evidence for the feasibility of developing AI-enabled quantitative endoscopy for airway CSA measurement.
item.dc:creator: Amirsajjad Taleban, Jake Luo, Christopher E. Larkee, B. Tucker Woodson, Ryan Puccia, John S. Rhee, Guilherme J. M. Garcia

item.title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.20671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.
item.dc:creator: Hem Raj Dadral Najam Ul Hasan, Naveed Ejaz, Muhammad Aslam Jarwar

item.title: Separating mixtures of single-fiber orientation distributions for increased sensitivity to crossing white matter fibers
item.description: arXiv:2610.20974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intro: Diffusion MRI allows for in vivo probing of brain tissue architecture via micron-level diffusion aggregated at the millimeter scale, but crossing white matter fibers decrease the sensitivity of downstream tasks such as microstructural modeling and tractography. Current fixel-based methods for identifying the number, orientation, and spread of fibers rely on finding the peaks of fiber orientation distributions from constrained spherical deconvolution. However, this method is biased by the spreads of nearby fibers and fails at angular separations lower than approximately 40-50 degrees. Methods: In this work, we perform a constrained nonlinear optimization called fiber segmentation by signal splitting and iterative least squares estimation (FISSILE), modeling each voxel as a mixture of single-fiber distributions. We use FISSILE to fit axially symmetric fibers in simulations and on three in vivo human subjects from the Human Connectome Project, an ex vivo raccoon brain, as well as the same human subject scanned twice at two different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Results: On simulated data, FISSILE successfully identifies fibers at an angular separation of 40{\deg} and a volume fraction of 0.1 at an SNR as low as 30, while MRtrix3's fod2fixel is limited to 60{\deg} separation and 0.1 volume fraction at the same SNR. On acquired data, FISSILE identified 85.8% of white matter voxels on average in human brains and 79.4% in the raccoon with at least one fiber crossing, whereas fod2fixel identified 30.1% and 44.5%. The number of white matter fiber crossings was mildly sensitive to different noise levels in the human subject with two acquisitions. Conclusion: A method that models the crossing fiber phenomenon as an unmixing problem increases sensitivity to individual fibers for more precise characterization of anatomy.
item.dc:creator: Adam M. Saunders, Gaurav Rudravaram, Michael E. Kim, Elyssa M. McMaster, Yifan Shuai, Warren Boschen, Sophie Lin, Suzana Herculano-Houzel, Daniel C. Colvin, Yurui Gao, Kurt G. Schilling, Adam W. Anderson, Bennett Landman

item.title: Evidence Field for Histopathology: Cross-Centre Evaluation and Replayable Spatial Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2610.21115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Histopathology classifiers must transfer across acquisition sites while exposing evidence that can be checked independently. Evidence Field couples learned image measurements and spatial classification with a native covering-program record. We evaluate this architecture on all 455,954 released CAMELYON17-WILDS patches, using patient-separated source partitions and two held-out hospital centres. Eighteen from-scratch fits compare four Evidence Field objectives with residual convolutional and compact vision-transformer classifiers. Checkpoints, temperatures and review thresholds are selected using source validation. The source-selected paired-cross-entropy ensemble achieves areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.9356 and 0.9453, with accuracies of 84.46% and 86.77% at the two held-out centres. Corresponding convolutional values are 0.7352 and 0.7656, and transformer values are 0.8502 and 0.7924. Evidence Field has 10,550 trainable parameters per member and additionally returns selected covers, signed region and interaction terms, contextual dependencies and independently reconstructible predictions. Patient-cluster intervals, calibration, source-fixed review policies and recorded training resources characterize the results. A 340-image, three-member audit reconstructs probability mixtures and 6,120 class programs under three rigid views. The evaluation supports cross-centre discrimination and reproducible computation for these implemented models; unequal family tuning, previously examined public targets and limited patient groups constrain broader interpretation.
item.dc:creator: Isarar Siddique, Raiyan Siddique, Arshi Niyaz, Jamyang Ugyen Tshomo, Atish Raza

item.title: Tokenized Joint Source-Network Coding for Loss-Resilient Video Streaming
item.description: arXiv:2610.21166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For decades, conventional video streaming systems have relied on packet-level forward error correction (FEC) codes and retransmissions to ensure reliable video delivery. However, in real-time communications, FEC is inherently inefficient under unknown and time-varying packet-loss conditions, while retransmission can incur excessive latency and fail to meet stringent playout deadlines. Emerging deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) provides an alternative by learning channel-noise-resilient representations, yet its tight coupling with the physical layer makes it difficult to integrate into today's layered network architectures and protocols. In this paper, we propose TokJSNC, a simple-but-effective tokenized joint source-network coding paradigm for packet-loss-resilient video streaming. Rather than first compressing video into a compact bitstream and then protecting it with packet-level FEC, TokJSNC directly encodes video into variable-length discrete token-stream, whose transmission rate is jointly adapted to video content complexity and network conditions. By exploiting the spatiotemporal correlations among learned video tokens, TokJSNC enables robust video reconstruction over a wide range of packet-loss rates without explicit FEC or retransmissions. Consequently, TokJSNC brings the JSCC-like graceful degradation property to the network layer while remaining compatible with existing network architectures and transport protocols. Experimental results show that TokJSNC maintains an average playback frame rate above 22 fps even at a 70% packet-loss rate, whereas the best-performing baseline drops below 12 fps. Overall, TokJSNC establishes a practical pathway for repurposing modern generative video tokenizers for loss-resilient streaming, while providing a fundamental framework for video token communications.
item.dc:creator: Ke Yang, Sixian Wang, Kailin Tan, Guo Lu, Jincheng Dai, Wenjun Zhang, Ping Zhang

item.title: Monotone Piecewise-Linear Harmonization of Multitemporal Multispectral Surface Reflectance With Unsupervised Deep Multiview Pseudoinvariant Features Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.21183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface reflectance products derived from optical satellite may exhibit systematic inconsistencies across acquisition dates, because atmospheric correction is generally performed independently for each image. Such residual biases distort the temporal behavior of invariant ground targets and reduce the reliability of multitemporal surface reflectance analysis. This study proposes Deep Multitemporal Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (DeepMGCCA), an unsupervised deep multiview pseudoinvariant feature learning framework that integrates Deep Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (GCCA) with Multivariate Alteration Detection (MAD) to identify deep-pseudoinvariant features (DIFs) for the removal of surface reflectance biases across multitemporal satellite observations. Unlike conventional MAD-based approaches that rely on linear GCCA, the proposed framework replaces date-specific linear projections with a shared convolutional encoder. The framework learns deep invariant features (DIFs) directly from pixel-weighted canonical variates via iterative reweighting strategy, while a reconstruction regularizer preserves surface reflectance information and prevents degenerate collapse from suppressing genuine temporal variability. Experiments were conducted on four annual Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 acquisitions across four regions of interest (ROIs) to evaluate four DIF-based harmonization transforms. A monotone piecewise-linear transform derived from DIFs quantiles consistently achieved the largest bias reduction, lowering the between-date spectral angle by up to 2.54 and RMSE by 0.015, and raising PSNR by up to 4.04~dB. These findings demonstrate the potential of deep invariant feature learning for multitemporal surface reflectance bias removal while highlighting the importance of preserving physically meaningful temporal and spectral information during nonlinear representation learning.
item.dc:creator: Lino Garda Denaro, Chia-Hsiang Lin

item.title: Bayesian Joint Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Limited-Data Multi-Contrast X-Ray CT
item.description: arXiv:2610.21406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-contrast X-ray computed tomography (CT) combines attenuation contrast with phase and dark-field contrast, which are sensitive to refraction and ultra-small-angle scattering, respectively. Common implementations record several intensity measurements per projection angle by phase or mask stepping, which lengthens acquisition and, at a fixed exposure per measurement, raises the dose. Limited-data acquisition via sparse angular sampling or reduced stepping lowers these costs but makes the data less informative, calling for prior information and uncertainty quantification. We study joint Bayesian reconstruction of attenuation, phase, and dark-field images from separately retrieved sinograms. A joint total variation term in the prior couples edge locations across the images but not their values. Posterior sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler complements maximum a posteriori estimates with pixel-wise uncertainty. We compare this joint prior with channel-wise total variation alone on synthetic and experimental Talbot-Lau interferometry data under full, sparse-angle, sparse-step, and combined acquisition (up to 24 times fewer exposures). Both maximum a posteriori reconstructions suppressed undersampling artifacts, with synthetic relative errors 1.6-11 times lower than those of filtered backprojection. The joint prior gave modest synthetic accuracy gains, a cleaner experimental dark-field background, 23-30 % lower mean dark-field posterior standard deviation, and 4-38% higher median effective sample size in experimental limited-data runs. In the synthetic study, posterior standard deviations matched or exceeded the errors in flat regions but underestimated them at boundaries, especially in phase. Experimental phase chains mixed slowly under angular undersampling. The formulation also applies to edge illumination with adapted forward and noise models.
item.dc:creator: Hassan Yazdanian, Henrik M\"akinen

item.title: Learning Variable Metrics for Convergent Proximal Splitting Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.22204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose learned variable metric (LVM), a framework that learns metrics of proximal splitting algorithms adapted to each problem instance, coordinate, and iteration with a convergence guarantee. Proximal splitting algorithms can solve a wide variety of convex optimization problems but often require many iterations to converge. Choosing a suitable metric is an effective remedy, and variable metric theory naturally extends convergence guarantees to metrics that vary over the iterations. Learning is a promising way to design such adaptive metrics beyond the reach of manual design, but a naive implementation leads to (i) an expensive evaluation of a network at every iteration and (ii) difficulty in satisfying the conditions that the theory imposes on the whole infinite sequence of metrics. To resolve these difficulties, we first train a neural network to generate a few representative metrics once per problem instance, and then obtain the metric of every iteration by combining them with basis functions of the normalized iteration index. We present LVM for the proximal gradient method with a quadratic term and the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, and prove their convergence under a mild spectral condition, which is ensured by a rescaling of the representative metrics. In experiments on deblurring and inpainting, LVM reduces the number of iterations to reach a target accuracy in most tested settings compared with several baselines, and the computation time at high accuracies.
item.dc:creator: Yodai Suzuki, Shunsuke Ono

item.title: Denoising Textures is a Different Ballgame Altogether!
item.description: arXiv:2610.22258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The human brain effortlessly deciphers colors and textures from visual stimuli and reconstructs the world around us, yet preserving such details remains challenging in image denoising. While significant progress has been made in generic image denoising, the problem of texture denoising has remained relatively under-explored. Fine details, such as intricate patterns and repetitive structures, often suffer from over-smoothing even in deep learning based approaches for denoising. In this paper, we analyze the behavior of state-of-the-art (SOTA) denoisers on texture datasets and show that performance improvements are possible only by fine-tuning the denoisers on the texture datasets. Surprisingly, fine-tuning on texture datasets result in the models catastrophically forgetting the original dataset. These findings highlight the need for specialized treatment of textures in denoising. Since denoising quality directly impacts downstream tasks such as generative modelling, we argue that dedicated texture aware denoisers are essential for faithful texture reconstruction and synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Saptarshi Mandal, Oindrila Haldar, Chirayata Bhattacharya, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula, Zhiwei Xu, Thrasyvoulos N. Pappas, Gaurav Sharma

item.title: Data-driven Smooth-to-hard Spectral Regularization for General Linear Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The logistic smooth-to-hard shrinker is the proximal map of an explicit saturating spectral penalty for general linear inverse problems. Its exact weak convexity yields a unique scaled update and proximal-gradient stationarity guarantees, while independent validation provides finite-grid parameter-selection control. We use MRI as an illustrative example.
item.dc:creator: Guanzhong Yang, Zi Wang, Guang Yang

item.title: PanoDiff-SR: Synthesizing Dental Panoramic Radiographs using Diffusion and Super-resolution
item.description: arXiv:2507.09227v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interest in generating realistic synthetic medical images has grown in recent years. Such datasets can mitigate the scarcity of public data for artificial intelligence research and support education. Work on synthesizing dental panoramic radiographs (PRs) has so far relied almost exclusively on generative adversarial networks (GANs), and three limitations recur: the synthesized field of view is often restricted to a cropped dentoalveolar region rather than a complete PR; observer studies of GAN-generated PRs report that clinicians still identify synthetic images with accuracies of roughly 78-82%, implying persistent visible giveaways; and adversarial training remains sensitive to instability and mode collapse. Generating a full-size PR directly at diagnostic resolution with a diffusion model is an alternative, but sampling at that resolution is costly. We therefore present PanoDiff-SR, an end-to-end two-stage pipeline developed and evaluated specifically for panoramic radiography: a denoising diffusion implicit model (PanoDiff) generates a low-resolution (LR) seed PR ($256\times128$), which a fine-tuned hybrid attention transformer (HAT) super-resolution (SR) stage upscales to a high-resolution (HR) PR of $1024\times512$. Decoupling the expensive generative step from the resolution step yields complete, full-arch PRs at diagnostic resolution on a single 47 GB GPU. The Fr\'echet inception distance between 7243 real and synthetic HR images is 40.5. Inception scores were 2.68, 2.38, 2.90 and 2.98 for real HR, synthetic HR, real LR and synthetic LR images, respectively. Six clinical experts, each evaluating 100 synthetic and 100 real PRs under a time limit, distinguished real from synthetic images with an average accuracy of 68.5% (50% corresponds to random guessing), substantially closer to chance than reported for GAN-based studies. Project page: https://s4nyam.github.io/panodiff/
item.dc:creator: Sanyam Jain, Bruna Neves de Freitas, Andreas Basse-OConnor, Alexandros Iosifidis, Ruben Pauwels

item.title: Absorption and Phase-Contrast Microtomography Using Direct X-Ray Detection With Commercial Off-The-Shelf CMOS Sensors
item.description: arXiv:2605.29808v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work presents high-resolution X-ray microtomography based on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) CMOS image sensors as direct detectors. The system uses a microfocus X-ray source in cone-beam geometry, enabling both absorption-contrast imaging, thanks to the sensor s intrinsic resolution, and phase-contrast imaging, by adjusting the object-to-sensor distance. A dynamic flat-field correction algorithm mitigates radiation-induced sensor degradation during long acquisitions. The setup provides voxel sizes from 3.9 microns to 5.2 microns, with an effective spatial resolution (FWHM) as fine as 9.6 microns in magnified phase-contrast mode (1.33x) and 21 microns in non-magnified absorption-contrast mode. Phase contrast enhances visualization of soft tissue boundaries that are difficult to visualize using absorption-contrast imaging in the same experimental configuration.
item.dc:creator: Damian L. Corzi, Jose Lipovetzky, Fabricio Alcalde Bessia, German Mato, Andres Cicuttin, Maria L. Crespo, Martin Perez, Mariano Gomez Berisso

item.title: Tile-Based Phase Unwrapping with Reliability-Ordered Joining and Residual-Weighted Multipath Averaging
item.description: arXiv:2609.13409v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Phase unwrapping recovers a continuous phase map from measurements known only modulo 2{\pi}, in the presence of noise and discontinuities. We propose a tile-based method that combines local spectral reconstruction, reliability-ordered tile joining, and residual-weighted multipath averaging. Each tile is reconstructed by a discrete cosine transform (DCT) least-squares solve, and robust measurements along tile borders guide their joining along a spanning tree. We repeat this reconstruction on shifted tile grids and on rotated and reflected copies of the image, which changes tile borders and joining paths. A residual-weighted average combines the resulting reconstructions, which are computed in parallel and averaged on the fly without being stored. We also introduce the corrected circular rewrapping error, a congruence measure: after removing a global phase offset, it measures how far the rewrapped reconstruction is from the observed phase. It applies to least-squares and path-based methods, even without an unwrapped reference. Used with reference-based errors, it separates agreement with the measurement from recovery of the correct number of cycles. Experiments on radar-interferometric, magnetic-resonance, holographic, and constructed phase images compare our method with seven reference algorithms. Among the methods that complete every test image, ours has the lowest mean fraction of pixels with an error above {\pi}. On the images all methods complete, it lies on several speed-accuracy Pareto fronts. Error maps also reveal isolated cycle errors that average scores or congruence alone can hide.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Moevus, Max Mignotte

item.title: MorphoBranch: A Fine-Structure-Preserving Workbench for Morphometric Analysis of Branched Cellular Structures
item.description: arXiv:2610.00860v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background and Objectives: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors provide readouts of neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes are prone to fragmentation and false connections that bias skeleton-based measurements. We present MorphoBranch, a fine-structure-preserving, human-reviewable workbench for morphometry of branched cellular structures. Methods: MorphoBranch combines a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine. The Mor- phometry Engine implements an image-to-graph workflow integrating multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmen- tation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, and graph-based morphometry. The Refinement Engine maps natural-language requests to registered actions for parameter adjustment, preview execution, metric reporting, and unsupported-request handling, while image processing and quantitative computation remain deterministic and reviewable. Results: MorphoBranch was evaluated on two public neuronal axon datasets, AxonMIP and AxonStack, and the in-house Cell- Morph dataset of microglial fluorescence images. It achieved the highest Skeleton F1 and clDice and the lowest length-estimation error among the evaluated methods on all three datasets, while also achieving the highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and Axon- Stack. Across 150 natural-language tasks, the Refinement Engine achieved a 94.0% end-to-end success rate. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that MorphoBranch provides a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for mor- phometric analysis of branched cellular structures. It supports fine-structure-preserving quantification across neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images while maintaining inspectable and reproducible analysis workflows.
item.dc:creator: Song Zhiying, Ling Hanyi, Wu Junyi, Jiang Yangbo

item.title: BOLT: Universal Classifier Training via a Bayes-Error Upper Bound
item.description: arXiv:2501.07754v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work introduces a novel approach to compute a universal upper bound on the Bayes error rate (BER) from classifier-output samples, which serves as a Bayes-error-related performance criterion for the underlying classification task. We show that the bound is tight in the binary case and characterize the max-sum gap that appears in the aggregate multiclass formulation. Based on this bound, we define a new loss function, called Bayes optimal learning threshold (BOLT), for training parameterized classifiers. For each data sample, the BOLT loss computes a term whose expectation upper-bounds the Bayes error, so that during training the model parameters can be updated toward minimizing this bound. Numerical experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets show that, in the reported settings, BOLT training often attains lower held-out classification error than cross-entropy training.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadreza Tavasoli Naeini, Ali Bereyhi, Morteza Noshad, Ben Liang, Alfred O. Hero III

item.title: Smooth Hard-Thresholding for Singular Values with Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate
item.description: arXiv:2606.06632v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-rank matrix denoising is a central primitive in patch-based image restoration and many other inverse problems. Classical SVD-based image denoising methods often choose a truncation rank by matching residual singular-value energy with an estimated noise energy, but this rule is not a finite-sample risk principle because a fitted low-rank approximation inevitably absorbs part of the noise. This paper develops a mathematically rigorous alternative based on Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE). Since singular value hard thresholding is discontinuous and does not satisfy the hypotheses of Stein's lemma, we introduce a logistic smooth hard-threshold spectral estimator. We prove that the smooth shrinker satisfies the regularity conditions required by a spectral-estimator version of Stein's lemma, and therefore admits an exactly unbiased fixed-threshold risk estimate under Gaussian noise. For a fixed observed matrix and a finite set of candidate thresholds separated from the observed singular values, the ordering of the fixed-threshold smooth SURE objective eventually agrees with a simple limiting score. The limiting score has the same algebraic form as the biased hard-threshold SURE formula, but here it is used only as a computational device for ranking finite candidates. Selecting the minimizing threshold is a data-adaptive tuning step; the selected SURE value should not be interpreted as an unbiased risk estimate of the finally selected estimator.
item.dc:creator: Guanzhong Yang, Zi Wang, Guang Yang

item.title: WHTMix: Efficient Stereo Depth Estimation via Walsh-Hadamard Token Mixing
item.description: arXiv:2607.25234v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stereo depth estimation for driving, robotics and augmented reality must run at high resolution under tight latency budgets, yet in transformer-based matchers the global self-attention that aggregates scene context grows quadratically with the number of pixels and comes to dominate runtime. We show that the joint self-attention stage of a stereo transformer, whose role is to spread context across both views, can be replaced by a data-independent Walsh-Hadamard token mixer that mixes tokens globally in the transform domain at log-linear cost, while the data-dependent cross-attention that performs left-right correspondence is retained. On synthetic driving data the mixer matches the attention baseline in end-point error while reducing model compute by a factor of 2.46 and single-image inference latency by a factor of 2.65. A complexity analysis shows the benefit is governed by the ratio of sequence length to channel width, which explains why high-resolution stereo matching is a particularly favorable setting and why classification transformers are not; we confirm this token-to-channel scaling on non-stereo long-sequence benchmarks. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid log-disparity loss function designed to up-weight small-disparity pixels corresponding to long-range objects. This approach reduces the error on distant objects without incurring any additional computational overhead.
item.dc:creator: Prathyush Sajith, Emadeldeen Hamdan, Ahmet Enis Cetin

item.title: A comparative assessment of global building and settlement datasets across geographic and settlement contexts
item.description: arXiv:2609.28154v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Global building and settlement products increasingly support population mapping, exposure assessment, and urban monitoring, yet comparative evidence remains fragmented across representations, geographic contexts, and evaluation methods. We benchmark seven global or near-global products against harmonized reference building footprints across 135 study areas. Our representation-aware framework integrates complementary measures of detection, geometric agreement, and aggregate quantity accuracy with stratified analyses of settlement characteristics, evaluation resolution, reference provenance, and temporal alignment. Overture Maps achieved the highest median city-level vector F1 (0.786), while 3D-GloBFP showed the closest aggregate building-area agreement despite weaker detection performance. Raster rankings were scale-dependent: Google Open Buildings Temporal (OBT) performed best at 10\,m (F1 = 0.680), whereas WSF Tracker led at 100\,m (F1 = 0.904) but substantially overestimated reference building area (relative bias = 1.845). Raster accuracy increased with building density ($\rho=0.58$--$0.75$), while smaller candidate footprints were disproportionately associated with vector false positives. Temporal alignment improved WSF Tracker mean city-level F1 by 0.060. These findings demonstrate that product reliability depends on representation, spatial scale, and settlement context, providing a reproducible framework for assessing the suitability of EO-derived urban information for different applications.
item.dc:creator: Rufai Omowunmi Balogun, Caroline Margaux Gevaert, Capucine Riom, Derrick Mirindi, Aaron Opdyke, Hamed Alemohammad, Pierre Chrzanowski, Edward Charles Anderson
